cues.text: The Jewish Feast of Weeks
Pentecost takes its name from the Greek word for "fiftieth," marking the fiftieth day after Easter Sunday.
It fell on the ancient Jewish harvest festival known as the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot), celebrated fifty days after Passover in thanksgiving for the wheat harvest.
In later Jewish tradition, the feast also commemorated the giving of the Law to Moses on Sinai.
That year, Passover had coincided with the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus.
The disciples were still gathered in Jerusalem for the feast when the events described in the second chapter of Acts took place.
Jerusalem in that season was crowded with pilgrims from across the Mediterranean and Near East, all there for the festival.
That detail becomes essential to what follows.
The Descent of the Holy Spirit
According to the Acts of the Apostles, the Eleven, the Blessed Virgin Mary, and other disciples were gathered together in Jerusalem.
Tradition places them in the same upper room where the Last Supper had taken place.
Suddenly a sound like a rushing wind filled the house, and what appeared as tongues of fire came to rest on each of them.
They began to speak in other languages, and the pilgrims gathered outside were astonished to hear Galileans preaching in their own native tongues.
Some onlookers mocked the disciples as drunk.
This prompted St. Peter to stand and address the crowd — the first recorded sermon of the Christian Church.
Peter's Sermon and the First Converts
Peter explained that what the crowd was witnessing fulfilled the prophecy of Joel, that God would pour out his Spirit upon all flesh.
He proclaimed that the Jesus they had crucified was both Lord and Christ, risen from the dead.
Acts records that the crowd was "cut to the heart" and asked what they should do.
Peter's answer was to repent and be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins.
Scripture presents this as the founding catechesis of the Church.

About three thousand were baptized that day, and the newly formed community devoted itself to the teaching of the Apostles the breaking of the bread the communal life and prayers described in Acts 2:42-47
Theological Significance
Catholic tradition regards Pentecost as the birthday of the Church.
It was the moment the Holy Spirit, promised by Christ before his Ascension, took visible possession of the community of believers and empowered them for their mission.
The confusion of tongues at Babel had once scattered humanity.
The gift of tongues at Pentecost is traditionally read as the opposite sign — that the Gospel would gather every nation back into unity.
The feast is closely tied to the Church's understanding of the sacrament of Confirmation, in which the same Spirit given at Pentecost is imparted to individual believers.
Liturgical Observance
Pentecost has been kept as a major feast since the earliest centuries of the Church, closing the fifty-day Easter season.
In the Roman Rite it is marked by red vestments, symbolizing the fire of the Spirit, and by the ancient sequence Veni Sancte Spiritus .
In English it was long known as Whitsunday , from the white garments worn by those baptized at the vigil.
The feast remains one of the principal solemnities of the liturgical year, second only to Easter and Christmas in importance.
It marks the Church's self-understanding as a community sent out to "make disciples of all nations."
